title: The lineage: what this paper came from, and where it opens

what.formal: A **lineage diagram** places a paper between its ancestors and its descendants: the work it depends on, the work it changes, and the directions its own open questions point toward. The ancestors here fall into five lines — spectral graph convolution, hypergraph convolution, gradient boosting, prior tree-with-network hybrids, and knowledge distillation — and the paper's contribution is the point at which two of them meet. The directions on the right are the six open questions from card 113, grouped into the four directions they point toward — each names work that this paper makes possible and does not do.
what.plain: The paper sits where three separate lines meet: convolutions on graphs, convolutions on hypergraphs, and boosted trees. Below it are the things it fixes, above it are the things nobody has done yet.

what.cap: The paper's lineage. Three ancestral lines — graph convolution, hypergraph convolution and gradient boosting — converge on the framework; a fourth and a fifth supply its protocol and its nearest rivals; four directions lead out from its own open questions.

what.md: **How to read it.** The left column is not a list of inspirations; it is a list of dependencies with different statuses. Two of the five supply something the paper **uses unchanged** — Equation (1) from HGNN, the boosting algorithm from Friedman — and those arrows are the paper's foundations. One supplies a **method the paper extends** — BGNN and DeepTLF, the prior attempts to feed trees to a network. One supplies the **protocol** its experiments are defined by. And one, GCN at the top, supplies nothing directly: it is there because HGNN is the hypergraph form of GCN's layer, so it is the ancestor one level removed.

example.md: **Walk 1 — trace one ancestor all the way to a number in a table.** Lineage diagrams are decorative unless they connect to results, so follow the top-left box.

items.md: GCN (2017) establishes that a vertex's features can be updated by a degree-normalised average over its neighbours, derived as a truncated spectral filter. The normalisation is the $1/\sqrt{d_i d_j}$ factor on pairwise edges.
items.why: The reason this matters is not historical. It is that the normalisation's *purpose* — preventing high-degree vertices from dominating — is what HGNN's $D_v^{-1/2}$ and $D_e^{-1}$ do for groups, and what makes Equation (1) numerically stable enough to stack.

items.md: HGNN (2019) generalises the relation from two vertices to any number, replacing the adjacency matrix with the incidence matrix $H$ and adding a second degree matrix $D_e$ for the relations themselves.
items.why: This is the paper's Equation (1), and it is used verbatim — one arrow from here to the middle box is solid because nothing about the operator changes. The paper's contribution is entirely in what the operator receives.

items.md: Follow the middle box's bottom-left line to a table. The iHGNN stage carries the operator unchanged, and the HGNN column of Table V is that stage running on the raw features — a column mean of $85.529$.
items.why: So the ancestor is measurable. The gap between $85.529$ and DD-HGNN's $87.648$ is what the two encoders and the fusion layer add on top of a component inherited intact from HGNN, which in turn is a generalisation of one inherited from GCN. **A lineage is only worth drawing when the inherited links are visible in the results, and here they are — as the row of the table labelled with the ancestor's name.**

example.md: **Notice the distribution.** Four of the six directions cost a day or less to pursue, and two of those are answerable by the authors from work they have already done — the timing table and the dataset name are outputs of runs that produced the paper. **This is a general feature of the literature and it is worth internalising: the questions a good paper leaves open are usually not the ones its authors could not solve, but the ones they did not stop to report.** That is why a lineage diagram's right-hand column belongs in a study site at all. It is not speculation about the future; it is a to-do list extracted from the present.

quiz.q: Which ancestor line contributes something to this paper **unchanged**, and which contributes only its protocol?

opts.md: Hypergraph convolution and gradient boosting contribute unchanged; GCN contributes its protocol
opts.expl: The pairing is inverted. GCN contributes nothing directly — its role is as the pairwise ancestor of HGNN's layer. The protocol comes from the distillation line, reference [34].

opts.md: Hypergraph convolution supplies Equation (1) unchanged and gradient boosting supplies the ensemble unchanged; the protocol comes from LightHGNN
opts.expl: Correct. Two components are inherited verbatim — the propagation operator from HGNN, and the boosting algorithm and its pre-trained trees from Friedman's line. The evaluation protocol, which defines what every number means, is inherited from reference [34]. Distinguishing what is inherited unchanged from what is modified is the fastest way to locate a paper's actual contribution: **here it is the two encoders and the fusion layer, and everything else was already built.**

opts.md: All five lines contribute ideas that were modified
opts.expl: The paper is explicit that the hypergraph network stage is left untouched, and its rule encoder uses a standard pre-trained GBDT. Nothing about either is modified — which is precisely why the contribution can be located entirely in the input to the network.

quiz.q: The lineage's two lowest-left arrows are GCN to HGNN to this paper. Using Table V's column means — GCN $84.805$, HGNN $85.529$ — what did generalising the convolution from pairs to hyperedges buy, in points, to three decimals?
quiz.hint: Both figures are column means over the same ten datasets. Subtract the smaller from the larger, and expect a value under one point.
quiz.sol: $85.529 - 84.805 = 0.724$ points on average across the ten datasets. Set that beside the $2.119$ points the knowledge embedding adds on top of HGNN and the proportion is worth noting: on these benchmarks the paper's own contribution is roughly three times the size of the architectural generalisation it is built on. That is not a criticism of HGNN — its largest single-dataset margin over GCN is $3.42$ points on Heloc — but it does calibrate what the two arrows in the left column are worth on average, which is the kind of comparison a lineage diagram makes possible and a results table does not.

quiz.q: Why is the eight-layer collapse in Table VIII best explained by the lineage rather than by the layer alone?

opts.md: Because GCN also collapses with depth, so the effect is inherited
opts.expl: The paper does not run GCN deep, so this is unavailable as evidence. The lineage explains the *mechanism*, not the observation — the operator's structure is inherited, so its failure mode is too.

opts.md: Because the operator inherited from HGNN has no residual connection, so each layer replaces rather than augments — and that design choice, not depth itself, is what makes the loss monotone
opts.expl: Correct. Tracing the operator back to the top-left box shows where the absence of a skip connection originates: the layer was designed as an averaging filter, where replacement is the intended behaviour. Table VIII's $43.19$-point loss is the price of a design that made sense for a two-layer filter and becomes pathological when stacked. **Lineage diagrams are useful for exactly this: they show which of a method's weaknesses are inherited rather than chosen, which is also what tells you whether a fix is yours to make.**

opts.md: Because the datasets in the lineage are the standard benchmarks
opts.expl: The eight-layer experiment is on CC-Cora alone, so the benchmark lineage does not bear on it. The relevant inheritance is architectural.

quiz.q: You are writing the related-work section of your own paper. What does this card's left column suggest you should provide?

opts.md: A chronological survey of the field
opts.expl: Chronology is the default and the least informative arrangement. Ordering by date tells a reader when things happened, which is rarely the question they have — they want to know which of these things you depend on and how.

opts.md: An account that distinguishes what you inherit unchanged, what you modify, and what you are replacing — with each dependency traceable to a specific part of your method
opts.expl: Correct, and the traceability is the part usually missing. Naming HGNN and GBDT as foundations is standard; making the dependency concrete — Equation (1) is used verbatim, the ensemble is pre-trained and frozen — is what lets a reader decide what your contribution actually is before they read your results. It also obliges you to be honest about a dependency's weakness, since an inherited component's failure mode is yours to live with even when it is not yours to fix.

opts.md: A list of every closely related method with a sentence each
opts.expl: A list is a bibliography with prose attached. It answers "what else exists" while leaving "what do you do differently" to be inferred, and the inference is exactly where a reader's effort should not be spent.
